summary: Written by the IAB, this document gives considerations for UNilateral Self-Address Fixing processes, where a host behind a NAT tries to learn the address others can reach it at. It lays out the problems and the conditions under which such techniques should be treated as short-term workarounds.

eli5.summary: Behind a NAT, a computer does not know its outside address, like not knowing your mailing address from inside a big building. This note warns that guessing tricks are risky and should be temporary.

questions: why are nat workarounds short term fixes
what did the iab say about nat
subtitle: The IAB explains why learning your own outside address from behind a NAT is only ever a short-term fix.

tldr.problem: Hosts behind a NAT do not know the address and port by which peers see them, and several proposals try to discover it unilaterally.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB lists the architectural and practical problems of these UNSAF processes and sets five things any such proposal must address: a limited scope, an exit strategy, brittleness, longer-term requirements and NAT experience.
tldr.outcome: Such workarounds MUST be treated as transitional in IETF protocols, with the intention to deprecate them when sound technical approaches are available.

today: RFC 3424 is an Informational IAB document from November 2002, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains a statement of the IAB's position that UNSAF techniques are transitional.

sections.title: The Self-Address Problem
sections.content:
Endpoints separated by one or more NATs do not know how to refer to themselves with addresses valid in their peers' address realms, because the translation is locked inside the NAT box. UNilateral Self-Address Fixing (UNSAF) is a process where an endpoint tries to determine or fix the address and port by which it is known, for example to use address data in a protocol exchange or to advertise a public address for incoming connections.

There are two cases. A client that starts communication creates an address binding in the NAT as a side effect. A server that only accepts connections creates no binding, so a mechanism is needed to fix one first.

The RFC is blunt: there are only heuristics and workarounds, no 100% solution. NATs may reclaim translations, so keep-alives and periodic re-polling may be required. Use of these workarounds MUST be considered transitional in IETF protocols.
sections.eli5: A computer behind a NAT is like someone inside a building who cannot see the street number others use to mail them. Guessing it can work for a while, but only as a stopgap.

sections.title: Architectural Issues
sections.content:
An UNSAF client asks an UNSAF service in a different address realm to reflect back the address it sees. The RFC lists the technical issues that block a general solution:

  • There is no unique outside to a NAT, so finding a suitable UNSAF server is hard.
  • An address is only valid relative to one point in the network, so another service may see a different one.
  • Without middlebox communication (midcom), circumventing the NAT may circumvent security mechanisms and expose internal machines.
  • With connectionless transports such as UDP, NAT bindings can change unpredictably.
  • Periodic refresh means both client and server must track presumed state.
  • The UNSAF server is not integrated with the middlebox, so it can only assume past behavior predicts future behavior.
  • Extra servers that must be reachable make the exchange more brittle.

Tight scoping helps: find the address from a specific service for use only with that service, and limit use to outbound requests to avoid unacceptable security exposure.
sections.eli5: There is no single outside, so each helper may see a different address for you. Helpers also add more things that can break.

sections.title: Practical Issues With Real NATs
sections.content:
Observation of deployed networks shows that NAT implementations vary widely. The RFC lists behaviors seen in practice:

  • NATs may drop fragments, since without complete TCP/UDP headers they may not create a mapping.
  • Application Layer Gateways (ALGs) depend on port numbers and can be hard to anticipate or undocumented.
  • Most NATs with ALGs for TCP protocols fail when strings to translate span multiple segments, and some fail with TCP options such as timestamps.
  • Many only work reliably with TCP, and timers that age out UDP flows vary widely.
  • Port numbers always change, and change unpredictably, and parallel NATs can change IP addresses too.
sections.eli5: Every NAT behaves a little differently, like each building having its own odd mail room rules. A trick that works in one may break in another.

sections.title: What an UNSAF Proposal Must Address
sections.content:
Because the IAB calls these approaches short-term fixes, any proposal must explicitly address five points:

  1. A precise definition of a specific, limited-scope problem. A short-term fix should not be generalized, since that prolongs dependence on it.
  2. An exit strategy or transition plan. Better fixes naturally see less use as proper technology arrives.
  3. Discussion of what makes systems brittle, for example using data at multiple network layers.
  4. Requirements for longer-term, sound technical solutions, and a contribution toward finding them.
  5. The impact of the practical NAT issues, with experience reports.
sections.eli5: If you want to use a temporary trick, you must say exactly what it is for, how you will stop using it, and what could break.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Appendices
sections.content:
UNSAF proposals may introduce security holes. In the absence of midcom there is no feasible way to let incoming communications through a firewall under proper supervision, as opposed to circumventing the firewall policies.

Appendix C gives examples. In one, a box A sits behind NAPT 1 and boxes B and C see its address differently: Box B sees some port on 10.1.2.27, while Box C sees an address in the space 192.168.3.0/24. A second example describes a home network with a broadband router and a later wireless access point with NAT enabled, leaving a wired and a wireless private realm.
sections.eli5: A trick that sneaks past the NAT can sneak past the security guard too. The examples show one device having different addresses depending on who looks.

viz.caption: THE FIVE CONSIDERATIONS FOR ANY UNSAF PROPOSAL

items.title: Limited scope
items.text: Define one specific problem and do not generalize the fix.

items.title: Exit strategy
items.text: Describe a transition plan so use fades as better technology arrives.

items.title: Brittleness
items.text: Discuss what makes the system more fragile.

items.title: NAT experience
items.text: Cover the practical issues with deployed NATs.
